section.title: Type Conversions — Python vs Java
section.subtitle: Every way to convert between types: numbers, strings, booleans, chars, collections and safe parsing.

topics.title: String → Number
topics.learn: Parsing text into int or float.

python.definition: int() and float() convert strings to numbers. They raise ValueError on invalid input — wrap in try/except or validate first.
python.code:
s = "42"
n = int(s)        # 42
f = float(s)      # 42.0

# safe parse
try:
    n = int("abc")
except ValueError:
    n = 0

# strip whitespace first
age = int(" 25 ")   # works — int() ignores spaces

java.definition: Integer.parseInt(), Long.parseLong(), Double.parseDouble() parse strings. They throw NumberFormatException on bad input — catch it or validate.

python.definition: str() converts any object to its string form. f-strings embed values directly into formatted text.
python.code:
n = 42
s = str(n)              # '42'
f = str(3.14)            # '3.14'

# f-string formatting
print(f"Value: {n}, Pi: {3.14159:.2f}")
# Value: 42, Pi: 3.14

# format specifiers
print(f"{255:#x}")      # hex → 0xff

java.definition: String.valueOf() or concatenation with + converts numbers to strings. String.format() and text blocks give formatted output.

topics.title: Character ↔ Number (ord / chr)
topics.learn: Converting between characters and their numeric codes.

python.definition: ord() returns the Unicode code point of a single character; chr() returns the character for a code point. Works for any Unicode character, not just ASCII.
python.code:
print(ord('A'))    # 65
print(ord('a'))    # 97
print(ord('€'))    # 8364 (Unicode!)

print(chr(65))     # 'A'
print(chr(97))     # 'a'
print(chr(8364))   # '€'

# char arithmetic
print(chr(ord('A') + 1))  # 'B'

java.definition: char is a 16-bit UTF-16 code unit. Casting (int)'A' gives the code; (char)65 gives the character. For full Unicode use codePointAt/codePointBefore.

python.definition: bool() converts any value to True/False. Falsy: None, 0, 0.0, '', [], {}, (). Everything else is truthy.
python.code:
print(bool(1))        # True
print(bool(0))        # False
print(bool(''))       # False
print(bool('hello'))  # True
print(bool([]))       # False
print(bool([1]))      # True

# explicit checks
if user_input:        # truthy check
    process()

# str ↔ bool
print(bool('True'))   # True (non-empty!)

java.definition: boolean is strictly true/false — no truthy/falsy concept. Boolean.parseBoolean() parses strings (only "true" ignoring case → true). Objects are never auto-converted.

topics.title: List/Array ↔ String
topics.learn: Joining collections into text and splitting back.

python.definition: str.join() combines iterables with a separator; str.split() breaks text into lists. list(map(str, nums)) converts numbers first.
python.code:
words = ['Python', 'Java', 'Go']
s = ', '.join(words)        # 'Python, Java, Go'

nums = [1, 2, 3]
s2 = '-'.join(map(str, nums)) # '1-2-3'

# split back
parts = 'a,b,c'.split(',')   # ['a','b','c']
lines = text.splitlines()

# str(list) is NOT join — gives repr
print(str([1,2]))   # '[1, 2]' not '12'

java.definition: String.join() combines CharSequence elements; String.split() uses regex. Arrays.stream().collect(joining()) works on streams and primitives via boxed types.

python.definition: Python has arbitrary-precision ints and one float type — no overflow, no explicit widening needed. int()/float() convert explicitly.
python.code:
i = 42
f = float(i)     # 42.0 explicit
i2 = int(3.99)   # 3 — TRUNCATES toward zero

# no overflow ever
big = 10**100    # works fine

# float→int loses decimals
print(int(-3.7)) # -3 (not floor!)
print(int(3.7))  # 3

java.definition: Java has fixed-size primitives: byte→short→int→long→float→double widen automatically (safe). Narrowing (double→int, long→int) requires explicit cast and may lose data.

python.definition: str() calls __str__() on any object — lists, dicts, custom classes all convert. repr() gives the developer/debug form.
python.code:
d = {'a': 1}
print(str(d))    # "{'a': 1}"
print(repr(d))   # "{'a': 1}" (same for dicts)

class Point:
    def __str__(self): return f'({self.x},{self.y})'
    def __repr__(self): return f'Point({self.x},{self.y})'

print(str(Point(1,2)))   # '(1,2)'
print(repr(Point(1,2)))  # 'Point(1,2)'

java.definition: String.valueOf(obj) or obj.toString() converts objects; StringBuilder/String.format for composition. Objects without toString() print class@hashcode.

topics.title: Collection ↔ Array / Other Collections
topics.learn: Converting between list, tuple, set, array.

python.definition: list(), tuple(), set() convert between built-in collections. No fixed-size arrays — lists are dynamic. array module exists for compact storage.
python.code:
t = (1, 2, 3)
l = list(t)          # [1, 2, 3]
t2 = tuple(l)       # (1, 2, 3)
s = set(l)          # {1, 2, 3} — dedupes!

# string ↔ list of chars
chars = list("abc")    # ['a','b','c']
word = ''.join(chars)   # 'abc'

# typed array (compact)
import array
arr = array.array('i', [1, 2, 3])  # 'i' = int

java.definition: Arrays.asList(), List.of(), new ArrayList<>(Arrays.asList(...)), and streams convert between arrays and collections. Primitive arrays need boxing (int[] ↔ List<Integer>).

python.definition: isinstance() checks types; try/except ValueError guards parsing. Type hints (def f(x: int)) document but don't enforce at runtime.

java.definition: The compiler enforces types — wrong types won't compile. instanceof checks at runtime; try/catch NumberFormatException guards parsing; generics prevent collection type errors.

python.definition: str.encode() → bytes; bytes.decode() → str. Encoding matters — UTF-8 is the default and handles all Unicode.
python.code:
s = "Hello "
b = s.encode('utf-8')      # b'Hello \xe4\xb8\x96\xe7\x95\x8c'
s2 = b.decode('utf-8')      # 'Hello '

# files
with open('f.txt', 'rb') as f:   # binary mode
    data = f.read()               # bytes
text = data.decode('utf-8')

# errors='ignore' skips bad bytes
b.decode('utf-8', errors='ignore')

java.definition: String.getBytes() → byte[]; new String(bytes) decodes. StandardCharsets.UTF_8 is preferred over string charset names. Files use Files.readAllBytes/write.
